::: {.tldr}
A single, calibrated score for every possible missense variant in the human proteome.
:::

{{< paper-links >}}

**Authors:** Rose Orenbuch, Courtney A. Shearer, Aaron W. Kollasch, Aviv D. Spinner, Thomas Hopf, Lood van Niekerk, Dinko Franceschi, Mafalda Dias, Jonathan Frazer & Debora S. Marks

## In brief

When a child with a severe developmental disorder has their genome sequenced, the cause is often a single changed letter in one protein. Finding it means telling apart the one harmful change from thousands of harmless ones. Many tools can rank variants within a gene that is already known to cause disease, but their scores are not comparable between genes, so they struggle with the many patients whose disease gene has not been discovered yet.

popEVE combines two sources of information. The first is evolution: by modelling the sequences of a protein across hundreds of species, our earlier model EVE learns which changes nature has tolerated and which it has removed. The second is human population data, which tells us how strongly each human gene is protected from damaging changes. Together they put every possible missense variant on one proteome-wide scale.

In a large cohort of children with severe developmental disorders, popEVE identified variants in 442 genes, including 123 that had not previously been linked to disease. It also ranked likely causal variants highly using only the child's exome, which matters wherever sequencing both parents is not possible.
